title: Chess notation
subtitle: How to read and write a move

blocks.title: Why you need notation
blocks.text: The whole of chess literature — books, puzzles, the games of the old masters — is written in one and the same language. Learn it and you can read any game ever played, and go back over your own moves.

The board has **coordinates**. The eight vertical columns — the files — carry the letters **a** to **h**, left to right as White sees them. The eight horizontal rows — the ranks — carry the numbers **1** to **8**, from the bottom up. Every square therefore has a name: the letter of the file first, then the number of the rank.

blocks.caption: The starting position. The white king stands on e1, the black king on e8. The square in the bottom right corner is h1 — and it is always light.

blocks.text: The pawn has no letter of its own. When you see only the name of a square — **e4**, **d5** — a pawn made the move. The letter of a piece is always **capital**, the name of a square always **lower case**, so the two are never confused. The knight takes **N** because K is already the king's.

items.title: e4
items.text: A pawn went to e4. Just the name of the square, with no letter in front of it.

items.title: Nf3
items.text: A knight went to f3. First the letter of the piece, then the square it arrived on.

items.title: Bxf7
items.text: A bishop **captured** a piece on f7. The **x** in the middle means a capture.
A plus at the end means **check** — the move attacks the enemy king.
A hash at the end means **checkmate**. The game is over.
Castling is written with a sign, not a square: **0-0** kingside, **0-0-0** queenside. Books and this app often write **O-O** with the letter O — it is the same thing.

items.title: When a pawn captures
items.text: The letter of the pawn's file goes before the **x**: **exd5**. Without it you cannot tell which pawn took.

items.title: Promotion
items.text: When a pawn reaches the end, the square is followed by **=** and the new piece: **e8=Q**.

blocks.title: Play 1.e4
blocks.hint: No letter of a piece, so a pawn moves — the one that lands on e4.
blocks.wrongMessage: Not that one. Look for the pawn that lands on e4.
blocks.playingPrompt: Play the move the notation describes.

blocks.title: Play 2.Nf3
blocks.hint: N is the letter for the knight.
blocks.wrongMessage: Wrong piece or wrong square. N is the knight, and it goes to f3.
blocks.playingPrompt: Play the move the notation describes.

blocks.title: Play Bxf7+
blocks.hint: The bishop captures on f7 and gives check at the same time: x is the capture, + is the check.
blocks.solvedMessage: That's it — Bxf7+. ✓ The notation is right — the sacrifice itself is not good here (Black takes with the king), but we only care how it is written.
blocks.wrongMessage: Not that one. Look for the bishop that captures on f7.
blocks.playingPrompt: Play the move the notation describes.

blocks.title: Play 0-0
blocks.hint: Castling is written with a sign, not a square — and it is played with the king.
blocks.wrongMessage: Castling is played with the king: move it from e1 to g1.
blocks.playingPrompt: Play the move the notation describes.

blocks.title: The same thing inside the app
blocks.text: A game is written down in pairs, with the move number in front: **1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6** means White played e4 first, Black answered e5, and then White brought the knight out to f3. The same record grows beside the board on the Game screen — with one difference: the app writes the piece letters in Serbian, so the knight is **S** and the bishop **L**. The shape of the record is exactly the one you have just learned.
